author: KERNAL Content Team
title: MLOps
subtitle: Tracking experiments, CI/CD for ML, and monitoring

whyItExists.problem: Without systematic practices, ML projects become chaotic: you can't reproduce a past experiment, you don't know which code version trained the model in production, different team members run conflicting experiments, and production models silently degrade.
whyItExists.solution: MLOps applies DevOps principles to machine learning: version experiments and data, automate testing and deployment, monitor models in production, and retrain when performance drops.
whyItExists.whenToUse: As soon as you have more than one model in production, more than one person working on ML, or when reproducibility and audit trails matter.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For pure one-off exploratory analysis or proof-of-concept notebooks that will never go to production.

explainModes.beginner: MLOps is like having a lab notebook for your ML experiments, automated tests for your models, and a system that watches your deployed models to make sure they still work well. It's DevOps but for machine learning.
explainModes.simple: MLOps means: track every experiment (what data, what model, what metrics), version your data and code together, automate testing before deployment, and monitor production models for quality degradation.
explainModes.standard: MLOps covers experiment tracking (MLflow), data versioning (DVC), ML pipelines, CI/CD for model deployment, and production monitoring. The maturity model goes from manual experiments → automated training → continuous deployment.
explainModes.technical: MLOps stack: MLflow for experiment tracking and model registry, DVC for data versioning, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, Evidently/Prometheus for monitoring. Reproducibility requires pinned dependencies, versioned data, and tracked random seeds.
explainModes.deepDive: MLOps maturity levels (Google/Microsoft): Level 0 — manual ML; Level 1 — automated ML pipeline; Level 2 — CI/CD for ML with automated retraining triggers. Feature stores (Feast, Hopsworks) decouple feature computation from model training, enabling consistent feature serving at training and inference time.

content.text: MLOps (ML + DevOps) is the practice of applying software engineering discipline to machine learning systems. It covers experiment tracking, data versioning, automated testing, CI/CD pipelines for model deployment, and monitoring in production.

items: Reproducibility — anyone can recreate any past experiment exactly
Automation — retraining and deployment happen without manual steps
Monitoring — production models are watched for quality degradation
Collaboration — team members can share, compare, and build on each other's work
Auditability — full history of which data trained which model in production

content.text: MLflow records every experiment run: parameters used, metrics achieved, and model artefacts saved. The MLflow UI lets you compare runs visually, pick the best model, and register it for deployment.

content.code:
import mlflow
import mlflow.sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, roc_auc_score
import pandas as pd

mlflow.set_experiment('churn-prediction')  # group runs by experiment

params = {
    'n_estimators': 200,
    'max_depth': 10,
    'min_samples_leaf': 5
}

with mlflow.start_run(run_name='rf-baseline'):
    # Log parameters
    mlflow.log_params(params)
    mlflow.log_param('training_rows', len(X_train))

    # Train
    model = RandomForestClassifier(**params, random_state=42)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Evaluate and log metrics
    preds = model.predict(X_test)
    probs = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    metrics = {
        'f1': f1_score(y_test, preds),
        'auc': roc_auc_score(y_test, probs),
        'accuracy': model.score(X_test, y_test)
    }
    mlflow.log_metrics(metrics)

    # Save model
    mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, 'model')

    print(f'F1: {metrics["f1"]:.3f}  AUC: {metrics["auc"]:.3f}')

# View all runs: mlflow ui   (opens at http://localhost:5000)

import mlflow
from mlflow.tracking import MlflowClient

client = MlflowClient()

# Register a model from a run
run_id = 'your-run-id'
mlflow.register_model(
    model_uri=f'runs:/{run_id}/model',
    name='churn-classifier'
)

# Promote to 'Staging' after review
client.transition_model_version_stage(
    name='churn-classifier',
    version=1,
    stage='Staging'
)

# Load from registry for serving
model_uri = 'models:/churn-classifier/Production'

content.text: Models degrade over time as the world changes. Data drift means the input distribution has changed. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the target has changed. Both require retraining.

content.code:
from evidently import ColumnMapping
from evidently.report import Report
from evidently.metric_preset import DataDriftPreset, ClassificationPreset
import pandas as pd

# Load reference data (what training data looked like)
reference_df = pd.read_parquet('data/train.parquet')
# Load current production data (last week of predictions)
current_df = pd.read_parquet('data/production_last_week.parquet')

# Data drift report
report = Report(metrics=[DataDriftPreset(), ClassificationPreset()])
report.run(
    reference_data=reference_df,
    current_data=current_df,
    column_mapping=ColumnMapping(target='churn', prediction='prediction')
)
report.save_html('drift_report.html')

# Check for drift programmatically
result = report.as_dict()
drift_detected = result['metrics'][0]['result']['dataset_drift']
if drift_detected:
    print('DATA DRIFT DETECTED — consider retraining')

content.definition: Open-source platform for tracking ML experiments, packaging code reproducibly, and deploying models. Provides a UI for comparing runs and a model registry for managing production versions.

A centralised repository for computed features that ensures consistency between training and serving. Prevents training-serving skew — the same features computed the same way. Tools: Feast, Hopsworks.

content.text: Version your training data as well as your code. A model is only reproducible if you can recreate the exact dataset used to train it. Use DVC to store data versioning metadata in git.

questions.question: What does MLflow track in an experiment run?
options: Parameters, metrics, and artefacts (model, plots) across runs for comparison
HTTP request logs from the API server
questions.explanation: MLflow tracks all parameters (hyperparameters), metrics (accuracy, F1), and artefacts (model files, plots) for each experiment run, enabling systematic comparison and reproducibility.

questions.question: What is data drift in an MLOps context?
options: When training data files are accidentally deleted
When the statistical distribution of production inputs changes compared to the training distribution
When the model's weights drift during long training runs
When different team members use different datasets
questions.explanation: Data drift occurs when the statistical properties of real-world inputs change over time, causing a model trained on historical data to become less accurate on current data.

questions.question: What is a Feature Store in MLOps?
options: A Git repository for storing feature engineering code
A centralised repository that ensures consistent feature computation between training and serving
A storage system for raw training data
A database that stores model predictions
questions.explanation: A Feature Store centralises feature computation so that features are computed identically during training and at prediction time (serving). This prevents training-serving skew, a common source of degraded production performance.

faq.a: A centralised repository for computed features that ensures consistency between training and serving. Training-serving skew (features computed differently at serving time vs training time) is a major cause of production ML failures. Tools include Feast (open-source) and Hopsworks.

faq.q: When should I retrain my model?
faq.a: Retrain when: (1) monitored metrics drop below a threshold, (2) data drift is detected, (3) new labelled data is available, or (4) on a fixed schedule (weekly, monthly). Automated retraining pipelines trigger on these conditions automatically.

faq.q: What is the difference between DVC and MLflow?
faq.a: DVC focuses on data and pipeline versioning — it tracks which dataset and code produced which model, integrated with git. MLflow focuses on experiment tracking and model management — logging parameters, metrics, and comparing runs. They complement each other well.
